label: Real run on this Mac's Docker Compose stack, with synthetic traffic from klaxon.traffic: synthetic data, a simulated provider, no real money. One fault from klaxon.faults, provider-outage, was injected on purpose. The alert was raised by klaxon.alerts from what the stack showed. Klaxon's loop ran live on it, through Claude Code on Aravind's seat, and stopped on diagnosed after 9 steps; any reply it got is a recorded response, not a simulation. It was offered one write action (rollback_deploy), as in week 4; in an evaluation run its gate only plans an action the diagnosis names: nobody is asked, and nothing runs. The diagnosis was compared with the fault's recorded cause by a rule (klaxon.grading), not by a person or a model. Its diagnosis named no action, so nobody was asked to approve one. The fault's cause was removed by the harness's clearing: this fault's cause is not a deploy.

case.name: provider-outage
case.title: Payments fail: the provider hangs, and our circuit breaker fails fast
case.right_answer: The fault's recorded cause: the provider's charge and refund API hangs (5 s, then 503): our payments API's calls to it time out, each after 3 attempts, until its circuit breaker opens, after 5 calls in a row got no answer; from then on it fails fast, answering 503 'outcome unknown' at once without calling the provider, and lets one trial call through 10 s after it opened, and again after each trial that fails.
case.remedy: nothing to change on our side: the provider must recover (escalate to it). Meanwhile the circuit breaker keeps the API answering at once, and closes again when a trial call gets an answer. After it recovers, the payments and refunds left pending need a decision (retry them with their keys, or mark them failed): a refund left pending blocks new refunds on its payment until it settles

alert.name: PaymentsErrorsHigh
alert.summary: Payments are failing: over the last minute, 97% of the answers to POST /payments on payments-api were 5xx (10.67 per second), above the threshold of 20%. Payments are slow: over the last minute, the p95 latency of POST /payments on payments-api was 3.7 s, above the threshold of 2 s.

diagnosis.hypothesis: The payment provider (fake-provider, an outside company) is degraded. It returned some 500s, and at 18:44:54 five calls in a row got no answer at all. That tripped the circuit breaker in payments-api, which runs with PROVIDER_BREAKER=on. Since then every 10 s half-open trial call has failed, so the breaker reopens each time. While it is open, POST /payments does not reach the provider: it leaves the payment pending and returns 503, which is the 97% 5xx rate. The 3.7 s p95 probably comes from requests that waited for provider timeouts before the breaker opened, plus the trial calls. This is an inference: the client histogram only records answered calls, and those were fast. No change on our side stands out. The whole stack was created together at 18:43:17 with what look like normal settings, so a rollback has nothing to undo. Still open: why the provider stopped answering, since we cannot see inside it, and the exact source of the 3.7 s latency.

evidence.shows: POST /payments is about 11.4/s 503 against about 0.26/s 201, confirming the alert. Refunds also return 503.
payments-api errors read 'provider unavailable; payment left pending' with '/v1/payments not sent: the circuit breaker is open'.
At 18:44:54 the breaker opened because '5 provider calls in a row got no answer'. Every half-open trial call since then failed and reopened it, at 18:45:07, 18:45:20, 18:45:33 and 18:45:46.
Provider calls returned 500s at 0.12 to 0.44/s alongside 200s from 18:43:46, then all calls dropped to 0 once the breaker opened.
Answered provider calls were fast (p95 under 35 ms). The failures were calls with no answer, which this histogram does not capture, rather than slow answers.
All services were created at 18:43:17 together. payments-api runs PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents and REFUND_CONNECTION=returned, so no single deploy explains the fault.
Provider attempts rose to about 4.5/s and then fell toward 0, matching the breaker cutting off calls.

proposed_fix.summary: No change on our side: the breaker is protecting us from a provider that is not answering. Escalate to the provider and check its status. Leave the breaker on; it will close by itself once a trial call succeeds. After recovery, reconcile the payments left pending (for example pmt_000411 to pmt_000426) with money_check, and make sure they are retried or resolved by their idempotency keys, not resubmitted blindly.

diagnosis.blast_radius: Doing nothing keeps payments and refunds failing with 503 until the provider recovers. Turning the breaker off instead would pile requests onto provider timeouts and could create duplicate or unknown-state charges.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: No change is made, so there is nothing to roll back. If someone later changes breaker settings, they can restore PROVIDER_BREAKER=on by redeploying payments-api with its previous settings.
